kurals.tamil:
கடன்என்ப நல்லவை எல்லாம் கடன்அறிந்து
சான்றாண்மை மேற்கொள் பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadanenpa nallavai ellaam kadanarindhu
saandraanmai merkol pavarkku.
kurals.meaning: For those who know what is due from them and take up the life of perfected character, every good thing is said to be simply their duty, something they do as a matter of course.
kurals.elementary: Some children help clear the table only when someone asks and then want a sticker for it. Others just do it every day because that is who they are. Valluvar says truly good people are like the second kind: being kind and helpful is not an extra for them, it is just their everyday job.
kurals.university: The chapter title saandraanmai (சான்றாண்மை, from saandror, 'the full, the accomplished', and aanmai, 'mastery, the bearing of a quality') names the fullness of noble character; the related noun saalbu (சால்பு, 'abundance, completeness') recurs throughout the chapter. The opening couplet turns on kadan (கடன், 'debt, duty'): for one who knows his kadan and undertakes (merkol, மேற்கொள்) saandraanmai, all good things (nallavai ellaam) are themselves called duty. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that for such a person all good things become 'natural duty' (இயல்பான கடமை), and Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan both render it as good qualities becoming one's very nature, the line of interpretation that follows the traditional commentary of Parimelazhagar, in which virtue is no longer a burden chosen case by case but an obligation already accepted. Pope's 'All goodly things are duties to the men, they say' keeps the reported-speech force of enpa (என்ப, 'they say'), marking this as received wisdom. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reverses the predicate ('the obligatory duty is the good things'), a minor variation in emphasis rather than in sense. The chapter follows Perumai (Greatness, ch. 98) in the Kudiyiyal and is followed by Panbudaimai (Courtesy, ch. 100). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that right action should be done simply because it is one's duty, not for what it brings.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise describes the perfected person as one for whom doing good is simply what is owed, not a bargain.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; strong match on goodness as duty, though the Gita's aim is liberation rather than the social ideal of the noble person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that even after doing everything commanded, they should regard it as no more than their duty.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats all good deeds as simply what is owed, leaving no room for self-congratulation.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on kingjamesbibleonline.org; a close match on good conduct understood as duty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents justice, good conduct and generosity as standing obligations upon the believer.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the whole range of good conduct is framed as something owed, not optional.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the alquran.cloud API; good thematic fit on good conduct as obligation, though it is a divine command rather than a description of the perfected character.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben Azzai said: Be quick in performing a minor commandment as in the case of a major one, and flee from transgression; For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai teaches that each good deed done as duty draws the next one after it, so that goodness becomes a way of life.
judaism.tie_back: This is how, in the Kural's words, all good things come to be the natural duty of one who has taken up the noble life.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:2 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong fit on goodness becoming habitual duty, framed in terms of commandments rather than character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As from a great heap of flowers many garlands can be made, even so should many good deeds be done by one born a mortal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges that a human life be used to do as many good deeds as possible, as a garland-maker uses every flower.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the doing of all good things as what a human being owes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a reasonable but partial match, urging good deeds without the Kural's explicit language of duty and character.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having adopted (the law), one should not hide it, nor forsake it.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga teaches that once the law of non-harm has been taken up, one must hold to it openly and never abandon it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's noble person likewise 'takes up' perfection (merkol) and then treats every good as a binding duty.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.4.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the match is on undertaking a moral law and holding to it as obligation, while the Acaranga's law is specifically ahimsa rather than all good qualities.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' fable of the Choice of Heracles, the young hero at a crossroads is approached by Vice, who offers an easy life of pleasure, and by Virtue, who offers a hard path of labour and duty; Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story presents the noble life as something a person deliberately chooses and then lives out through toil.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles' choice mirrors the Kural's person who knowingly takes up perfection and accepts all good things as duty.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus' Choice of Heracles, as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not quoted; captures the deliberate undertaking of virtue but not the Kural's point that goodness then becomes second nature.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyreplayers by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that moral virtues are formed by habit, so that doing good repeatedly makes goodness part of one's character.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains how, for the Kural's noble person, all good things become natural duty once perfection has been taken up.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong philosophical match on virtue becoming second nature, without the Kural's framing of goodness as debt.

kurals.tamil:
குணநலம் சான்றோர் நலனே பிறநலம்
எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kunanalam saandror nalane piranalam
ennalaththu ulladhooum andru.
kurals.meaning: The real excellence of the noble is the excellence of their character; every other kind of excellence does not count among true goods at all.
kurals.elementary: A shiny new bike, a nice haircut or a fancy pair of shoes can look great. But Valluvar says the thing that really makes a person beautiful is a kind and honest heart. Everything else is just wrapping paper.
kurals.university: The couplet sets kunanalam (குணநலம், 'the goodness of qualities, beauty of character') against piranalam (பிறநலம், 'other goods'). The noble (saandror) have only one nalam (நலம், 'good, beauty, excellence') worth the name; the other kinds are not counted 'among any good' (ennalaththu ulladhooum andru, எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று), where ulladhooum shows the alapedai (vowel lengthening) that fills out the metre. Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi read nalam as beauty (அழகு), contrasting inner beauty of character with outward beauty of form, while Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the more general 'good'; Pope's prose rendering, following the older commentarial tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, understands the other goods as sensual delights. Both readings make the same claim: for the perfected person only character counts. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama tells the boy Naciketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) are two different things; the wise person chooses the good, while the fool chooses the pleasant for the sake of gain and comfort.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad separates true good from attractive but lesser goods and praises the one who prefers the former.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that only the good of character is real good, and the rest do not count.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1-2 (cf. tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; a strong structural match on true good versus apparent goods, though the Upanishad's 'good' is liberation rather than moral character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
christianity.explanation: When Samuel is impressed by a tall, handsome candidate for king, God tells him that what matters is the heart, not appearance.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks inner character above every outward excellence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; strong match, especially with the commentators who read nalam as beauty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that outward looks and riches carry no weight with God; only the heart and conduct do.
islam.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's claim that character is the only real good and other goods do not count.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a near one-to-one match on inner worth versus outward goods.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thus said GOD: Let not the wise glory in their wisdom; Let not the strong glory in their strength; Let not the rich glory in their riches. But only in this should one glory: In being earnestly devoted to Me. For I GOD act with kindness, Justice, and equity in the world; For in these I delight —declares GOD.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah dismisses wisdom, strength and wealth as grounds for pride and points instead to kindness, justice and equity.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets aside every other excellence in favour of goodness of character.
judaism.source: Jeremiah 9:22-23 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Revised JPS 2023); strong match, though the prophet frames true glory as devotion to God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful. But he in whom these are wholly destroyed, uprooted and extinct, and who has cast out hatred — that wise man is truly accomplished.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that eloquence and good looks do not make a person accomplished; only freedom from jealousy, selfishness, deceit and hatred does.
buddhism.tie_back: This closely echoes the Kural's view that the accomplished person's only real excellence is character.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; near one-to-one, even sharing the idea of the 'accomplished' person.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a Brahmin priest that religious status comes from inner qualities, not from outward marks like shaved heads, mantras or forest dwelling.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that only goodness of character makes a person truly noble.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); strong match on inner quality over outward marks, set in a monastic rather than a householder context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At his trial Socrates says that his whole mission has been to urge people to care for the soul before body or property.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes virtue the one real good on which every other good depends.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; strong match, though Socrates makes other goods flow from virtue rather than denying them the name of good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant opens the First Section of the Groundwork by saying that nothing in the world, or even out of it, can be called good without qualification except a good will; talents, fortune and even health can become bad when the will that uses them is not good.
philosophy.explanation: Kant argues that every other excellence is only conditionally good, while goodness of will is good in itself.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in philosophical form: only goodness of character is good in every case.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (tr. T. K. Abbott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; a close conceptual match on character as the only unconditional good.

kurals.tamil:
அன்புநாண் ஒப்புரவு கண்ணோட்டம் வாய்மையொடு
ஐந்துசால் ஊன்றிய தூண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anbunaan oppuravu kannottam vaaimaiyodu
aindhusaal oondriya thoon.
kurals.meaning: Love, a sense of shame at wrongdoing, generosity to all, kindly regard for others and truthfulness are the five pillars on which perfect character rests.
kurals.elementary: Think of a tree house held up by five strong posts. If one post breaks, the house wobbles. Valluvar says a good person is held up by five posts too: loving others, feeling shy about doing wrong, sharing, being kind, and telling the truth.
kurals.university: This is the chapter's architectural image: saalbu (perfection) is a load resting on five pillars (aindhu ... oondriya thoon, ஐந்து ... ஊன்றிய தூண்). The five are anbu (அன்பு, 'affection'), naan (நாண், 'shame', specifically recoil from blameworthy deeds, as Pappaiah glosses பழி பாவங்களுக்கு நாணுதல்), oppuravu (ஒப்புரவு, 'benevolence to all, sharing what one has gathered', the subject of ch. 22), kannottam (கண்ணோட்டம், 'kindly regard', literally 'running of the eye', the subject of ch. 58) and vaaimai (வாய்மை, 'truthfulness', ch. 30). Commentators differ on how to parse saal: most take ஐந்து சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண் as 'the five pillars that bear saalbu', while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as pillars of the 'vessel' of perfection; Pope renders 'pillars five of perfect virtue's resting-place'. Karunanidhi glosses oppuravu as 'honouring the world's conduct' and kannottam as 'compassionate acts', showing how the virtues shade into each other. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Gita 16.1-3 Krishna lists the 'divine qualities' (daivī sampad) of the person born for liberation, among them fearlessness, charity, nonviolence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion for all beings, gentleness, modesty and forgiveness.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita gives a catalogue of virtues that together make up a godly character.
hinduism.tie_back: Several of the Kural's five pillars (love, shame, giving, kindness, truth) appear in this list as the supports of a noble nature.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.1-3 (cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; a good thematic match on a list of virtues, though the Gita's list is far longer than five.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists the qualities that grow in a person led by the Spirit.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's five pillars, it names a set of linked virtues, beginning with love, that together make up a complete character.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a reasonable structural parallel, though the lists only partly overlap and Paul's is presented as the work of the Spirit.

islam.quote_or_event: “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and for freeing slaves; [and who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; [those who] fulfill their promise when they promise; and [those who] are patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous.”
islam.explanation: The verse defines true righteousness through a set of pillars: faith, generous giving, prayer, keeping promises and patience.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes righteousness as resting on several supports, notably generosity and truthfulness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the alquran.cloud API; good structural fit, though its pillars include belief and ritual, which the Kural's list does not.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shimon the Righteous was one of the last of the men of the great assembly. He used to say: the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon the Righteous names the three supports on which the whole world stands.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of supports, with five pillars bearing up perfect character.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the shared image of pillars is striking, but the content (Torah, worship, acts of piety) only partly matches the Kural's five virtues.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One in whom there is truthfulness, virtue, inoffensiveness, restraint and self-mastery, who is free from defilements and is wise — he is truly called an Elder.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the true Elder by a short list of qualities rather than by age.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a handful of virtues, including truthfulness, as what makes someone truly accomplished.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a good structural match on a list of defining virtues, with truthfulness and inoffensiveness overlapping the Kural's list.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra defines the vows (vrata) as abstaining from injury, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and possessiveness, and says they are kept partially by householders (anuvrata) and completely by ascetics (mahavrata).
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics rests on five vows, which together form the backbone of a disciplined life for monks and laypeople alike.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's five pillars, the five vows are presented as the supports of a perfected character, with truthfulness common to both lists.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.1-2 (cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; the parallel of five supporting virtues is real, but only truthfulness and (implicitly) love through non-injury overlap with the Kural's five.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Book IV of the Republic, Socrates says that a perfectly good city must be wise, courageous, temperate and just, and then finds the same four virtues in the well-ordered soul.
greek_mythology.explanation: Plato's four cardinal virtues are presented as the components that together make up complete goodness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's five pillars, they name a fixed set of virtues on which a perfect character rests.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; next-best match only, since the shared feature is a numbered list of virtues while the virtues themselves differ.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The foundation of justice, moreover, is good faith; — that is, truth and fidelity to promises and agreements.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero names the two bonds that hold human society together: justice, and its close kin charity, 'which may also be called kindness or generosity' (I.20). He then rests justice itself on good faith, meaning truth and keeping one's word (I.23).
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Cicero rests good character on a few named supports, among them generosity, kindness and truth.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.20-23 (tr. Walter Miller)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Miller, Loeb 1913, I.23; I.20 phrase also checked). Partial match: generosity, kindness and truth overlap with the Kural's five pillars, but Cicero gives no list of five and does not include love or shame here.

kurals.tamil:
கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை பிறர்தீமை
சொல்லா நலத்தது சால்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kollaa nalaththadhu nonmai pirardheemai
sollaa nalaththadhu saalbu.
kurals.meaning: Austerity rests on the goodness of not killing; perfection rests on the goodness of not speaking of other people's faults.
kurals.elementary: A good person does not hurt any living creature, not even a bug. And a really good person also does not go around telling everyone the bad things someone else did. Valluvar says the first is the heart of being holy, and the second is the heart of being truly good.
kurals.university: A balanced couplet built on two parallel phrases: kollaa nalam (கொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not killing') grounds nonmai (நோன்மை, 'austerity, penance', glossed as தவம் by Varadarasanar and Kesikan), while sollaa nalam (சொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not telling') grounds saalbu. Pirar theemai (பிறர்தீமை) may mean either others' faults or the wrongs others have done; Karunanidhi takes the second ('not pointing out the harm others do'), the majority the first. The pairing ties this chapter to Kollaamai (ch. 33) and Purangooraamai (Not Backbiting, ch. 19), and suggests that just as non-killing is the essence of the ascetic, refusal to broadcast faults is the essence of the noble householder. Pope's 'penitence' for nonmai is archaic; 'austerity' is closer. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nonmai more broadly as 'sustaining life without destroying'. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of the body consists in worship of the Supreme Lord, the brāhmaṇas, the spiritual master, and superiors like the father and mother, and in cleanliness, simplicity, celibacy and nonviolence.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita counts nonviolence among the elements of bodily austerity (tapas), and the next verse adds truthful, non-agitating speech as austerity of speech.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links tapas with non-harm and, in the following verse, with restraint in speech.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good match on nonviolence as part of austerity, though the Gita's list is broader and the Kural makes non-killing its very essence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.”
christianity.explanation: James forbids believers to speak evil of one another, treating such talk as a usurpation of judgment.
christianity.tie_back: This directly matches the Kural's second clause: perfection lies in not speaking of others' faults.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a close match for the second half of the couplet, with no parallel to the first half on non-killing.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite each other. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares backbiting to eating a dead brother's flesh.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats talking about others' faults as a grave failure of character.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the alquran.cloud API; strong match for the second clause only.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not deal basely with members of your people. Do not profit by the blood of your fellow: I am GOD.”
judaism.explanation: Leviticus forbids slander and talebearing (the translators note 'deal basely' as, for example, slander) and, in the same verse, standing idly by another's blood.
judaism.tie_back: The verse pairs a ban on harmful speech with a concern for life, much as the Kural pairs not speaking ill with not killing.
judaism.source: Leviticus 19:16 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Revised JPS 2023, whose footnote glosses the idiom as slander or talebearing); notable because it joins speech and bloodshed in one verse, though the second clause concerns not profiting from a neighbour's danger rather than non-killing as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one's own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to stop examining other people's failings and to look at their own.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's teaching that perfection lies in not speaking of others' faults.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a strong match for the second clause.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future, all say thus, speak thus, declare thus, explain thus: all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.”
jainism.explanation: The Acaranga states the core Jain law of ahimsa: no living being may be killed, harmed or abused.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first clause in its most rigorous form: non-killing as the very ground of ascetic discipline.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.4.1.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near-exact match for 'austerity rests on non-killing', though it does not address the second clause on speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Book XV of Ovid's Metamorphoses, the philosopher Pythagoras urges people to stop killing animals for food, arguing that all souls pass between bodies and that slaughter defiles human beings.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pythagoras, a semi-legendary Greek sage, made abstention from killing a central religious discipline.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's view that real austerity begins with not killing.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV.60-478 (trans. A. S. Kline)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; next-best match, since it is a Latin poet's portrait of a Greek philosopher and addresses only the first clause.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises keeping silent for the most part and, if one must speak about other people, not to blame them, praise them or compare them.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic teacher counts restraint in speaking about others as part of the disciplined life.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's teaching that the noble do not talk about other people's faults.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; matches the second clause, though Epictetus also discourages praise and comparison.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல் அதுசான்றோர்
மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral panidhal adhusaandror
maatraarai maatrum padai.
kurals.meaning: The real strength of the capable is humility; it is the weapon with which the noble turn their enemies from enmity.
kurals.elementary: When someone is cross with you, shouting back usually makes it worse. But if you speak gently and say sorry, the angry person often calms down and even becomes your friend. Valluvar says being humble is the strongest tool a good person has.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the root aatru (ஆற்று, 'to accomplish, to be able'): aatruvaar aatral (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல்), 'the power of those who can achieve', is panidhal (பணிதல், 'bending, humility'). In the second line maatraar (மாற்றார், 'adversaries') are 'changed' (maatrum, மாற்றும்) by this padai (படை, 'weapon, army'), a deliberate pun. Most modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) read the second line as humility turning enemies away from enmity; Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan, nearer the older commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, read the first line more concretely as the achiever's skill in winning over helpers by bowing to them. Pope's 'Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sage / With that same weapon stills his foeman's rage' captures both senses. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Humility; pridelessness; nonviolence; tolerance; simplicity; approaching a bona fide spiritual master; cleanliness; steadiness; self-control; renunciation of the objects of sense gratification; absence of false ego; ... all these I declare to be knowledge, and besides this whatever there may be is ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places humility and pridelessness first in his list of the marks of true knowledge.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humility the first strength of the accomplished person.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 13.8-12 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io (abridged with ellipsis); matches the primacy of humility but not the Kural's image of humility disarming enemies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb observes that gentleness defuses anger while harshness inflames it.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim that humility is the weapon that turns adversaries from hostility.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; strong match on gentleness disarming hostility, though it speaks of soft words rather than humility as such.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that answering hostility with something better can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that the noble person's weapon changes enemies.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the alquran.cloud API; near one-to-one on transforming enemies, though the means is 'what is better' rather than humility specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: Avot de-Rabbi Natan expands the Mishnah's question 'Who is mighty?' by answering that the mightiest of the mighty is the one who makes an enemy into a friend.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition redefines strength as the power to win over one's adversary.
judaism.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's idea of the noble person's power to change enemies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; a strong match on strength as turning enemies into friends, though humility is not named as the means.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that enmity ends only when it is met without enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the way to end hostility is not counter-force but a gentler disposition.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; strong match on disarming enmity, though non-hatred rather than humility is the means.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Bravo! you have conquered anger; bravo! you have vanquished pride; bravo! you have banished delusion; bravo! you have subdued greed. Bravo for your simplicity, O saint! bravo for your humility, O saint! bravo for your perfect patience! bravo for your perfect liberation!”
jainism.explanation: After testing King Nami, who had renounced his throne, the god Sakra praises him for conquering pride and for his humility and patience.
jainism.tie_back: Nami's victory, won by humility rather than armies, parallels the Kural's view that humility is the true strength of the capable.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best match, since it praises humility as a conquest of the self but does not show humility winning over an enemy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable of the North Wind and the Sun, the Wind tries to strip a traveller's cloak by force and only makes him clutch it tighter, while the Sun's gentle warmth makes him take it off willingly.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable teaches that gentleness achieves what force cannot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents a gentle, unforced approach as the stronger weapon.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop's Fables, The North Wind and the Sun (Perry Index 46)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the well-known fable, not verified against a specific translation in this session; matches gentleness over force, but the 'enemy' is only a traveller.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they;--it is thus that they are the kings of them all.”
philosophy.explanation: Laozi teaches that the sea rules the streams because it lies lower than they do, and that the sage leads by placing himself below others.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's paradox in Daoist form: lowliness is the source of real power.
philosophy.source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching 66 (trans. James Legge)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on humility as power, without the Kural's specific point about winning over enemies.

kurals.tamil:
சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின் தோல்வி
துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Saalbirkuk kattalai yaadhenin tholvi
thulaiyallaar kannum kolal.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what the touchstone of perfection is, it is the willingness to accept defeat even at the hands of those who are not one's equals.
kurals.elementary: It is easy to say 'You win' to a big champion. It is much harder to say it to a younger child who beat you at a game. Valluvar says being able to lose gracefully, even to someone smaller, is the real test of a good person.
kurals.university: Kattalai (கட்டளை) here is the touchstone (உரைகல்) used to test gold, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss it: saalbu is gold, and its test is tholvi ... kolal (தோல்வி ... கொளல், 'accepting defeat'). Thulai allaar (துலையல்லார்), literally 'those not of the same balance (thulai, துலை)', are one's inferiors; the particle -um in kannum (கண்ணும், 'even with') makes the point that yielding to a superior is no test at all. Kesikan spells out the contrast: the defeat one would accept from one's betters must be accepted even from lesser people. Pope's verse ('What is perfection's test? The equal mind. / To bear repulse from even meaner men resigned') introduces 'equal mind' as a gloss rather than a translation. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thulaiyallaar as those 'unfit to accept defeat', a less common construal. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat – and by so doing you shall never incur sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna asks Arjuna to act with an even mind toward victory and defeat alike.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's touchstone similarly asks for a mind that can accept defeat without wounded pride.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.38 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; next-best match, since the Gita's equanimity concerns battle and duty, not yielding gracefully to an inferior.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?”
christianity.explanation: Paul rebukes Christians who sue one another and asks why they do not simply accept being wronged.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats willingness to lose to another as a mark of mature character.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; strong match on accepting defeat rather than insisting on winning, though without the Kural's specific reference to inferiors.

islam.quote_or_event: “I guarantee a house in the surroundings of Paradise for a man who avoids quarrelling even if he were in the right, a house in the middle of Paradise for a man who avoids lying even if he were joking, and a house in the upper part of Paradise for a man who made his character good.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet promises reward to those who give up an argument even when they are right.
islam.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's test of perfection: being willing to yield even when one could win.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4800 (graded hasan by al-Albani; Sunnah.com)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong match on yielding in a dispute one could win, and it ends by praising good character.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that those who are insulted but do not insult in return, who hear themselves shamed and do not answer, who act out of love and rejoice in suffering, are the ones of whom Scripture says, 'May those who love Him be like the sun rising in its might.'
judaism.explanation: The sages praise the person who absorbs humiliation without retaliating, comparing them to the rising sun.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees the willingness to take a loss without hitting back as the mark of the truly great.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; strong match on bearing defeat and insult without retaliation, though inferiors are not specified.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that winning breeds resentment and losing breeds pain, and that the peaceful let go of both.
buddhism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's view that a noble person does not need to win and can accept defeat calmly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; good match on freedom from the need to win, without the Kural's emphasis on yielding to inferiors.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira lists abuse (akrosha) among the hardships a monk must bear calmly, without anger or retaliation.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's touchstone, it asks one to accept humiliation even from those who are spiritually beneath one, without answering back.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on bearing defeat at the hands of a lesser person, though framed as monastic forbearance rather than a test of character.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Gorgias, Socrates shocks his hearers by maintaining that it is better to suffer wrong than to do wrong, and that he would choose to be wronged rather than wrong another.
greek_mythology.explanation: Socrates holds that losing to injustice harms only one's fortune, while committing injustice harms one's soul.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This gives a philosophical basis for the Kural's view that accepting defeat is a sign of a well-formed character.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; next-best match, since the Gorgias concerns suffering injustice rather than gracefully accepting defeat from inferiors.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is grievous, when a candidate for public offices, to be defeated by one's inferiors; therefore let him be defeated by Vatinius … That all men may know that these things, which I have deemed Cato worthy to undergo, are not real evils.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca has Nature explain why she put Cato through every hardship, including losing an election to the inferior Vatinius: to show that such defeats are no true evil to a good man.
philosophy.tie_back: Cato's calm acceptance of defeat by a lesser man is just the touchstone of perfection the Kural names.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Providence (De Providentia) 3.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Providence). The Wikisource text has no section numbers; 3.14 is the standard Latin reference (a deterioribus … Vatinio postferatur). Strong match on accepting defeat by inferiors, though Seneca presents it as a trial set by Nature rather than as a test of one's own humility.

kurals.tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்
என்ன பயத்ததோ சால்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Innaasey thaarkkum iniyave seyyaakkaal
enna payaththadho saalbu.
kurals.meaning: What use is perfect character if it does not do kind things even to those who have done one harm?
kurals.elementary: Being nice to people who are nice to you is easy. Valluvar asks a harder question: what if someone was mean to you? He says that being kind back to them is what really shows you are a good person.
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: if one does not do iniyavai (இனியவை, 'pleasant, kind things') even to those who did innaa (இன்னா, 'painful, harmful things'), of what use (enna payaththadho, என்ன பயத்ததோ) is saalbu? The -um of thaarkkum (தார்க்கும், 'even to those who did') carries the force. It restates for the noble householder the teaching of Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314 (inna seydhaarai oruththal avar naana nannayam seydhu vidal), and all modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Karunanidhi, Kesikan) agree on the plain sense. Note that the English section for this couplet on ytamizh.com is misaligned: its 'Couplet Explanation' belongs to Kural 946 on overeating and the line printed as the couplet is Pope's prose explanation, so it should not be relied on here. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled, and engaged in devotional service with determination, his mind and intelligence fixed on Me – such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the dear devotee as one who bears no hatred toward any being and is friendly and forgiving.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's call for kindness extended to all, including those who give offence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 12.13-14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a reasonable but partial match, as it describes universal friendliness and forgiveness rather than actively doing good to those who harm.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;”
christianity.explanation: Jesus commands his followers to love and do good to those who hate and harm them.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's demand to do kindness to those who have done harm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a near one-to-one match.

islam.quote_or_event: “Repel, by [means of] what is best, [their] evil. We are most knowing of what they describe.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells the Prophet to answer the evil done to him with what is best.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural's teaching of returning good for harm.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the alquran.cloud API; a close match on answering evil with good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat; If he is thirsty, give him water to drink. You will be heaping live coals on his head, And GOD will reward you.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs instructs that an enemy in need should be fed and given drink.
judaism.tie_back: This is a concrete form of the Kural's demand to do good even to those who have done harm.
judaism.source: Proverbs 25:21-22 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Revised JPS 2023); a close match, though the 'coals' image adds a note of the enemy's shame that the Kural also shares in Kural 314.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Overcome the angry by non-anger; overcome the wicked by goodness; overcome the miser by generosity; overcome the liar by truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that each kind of wrongdoing should be met with its opposite virtue.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that the wicked are to be met with goodness, not with retaliation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match on answering the wicked with goodness.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain account of Mahavira's ascetic years, the venomous serpent Chandakaushika bites the meditating Mahavira; instead of anger, Mahavira responds with calm compassion and words of awakening, and the snake gives up violence.
jainism.explanation: The story shows the Jina returning only compassion to a creature that tried to kill him, and thereby transforming it.
jainism.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural's question: what use is perfection if it does not do good even to one who does harm?
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, Parva X (Life of Mahavira) (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the well-attested Svetambara narrative, not verified verbatim or by section number in this session; a strong match on returning good for harm, framed as compassion (karuna) rather than a positive favour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Awaiting execution, Socrates tells Crito that it is never right to return wrong for wrong.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shares the Kural's rejection of retaliation, though the Kural goes further in demanding active kindness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; strong on non-retaliation but stops short of the Kural's positive kindness to the wrongdoer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “(It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting; to conduct affairs without (feeling the) trouble of them; to taste without discerning any flavour; to consider what is small as great, and a few as many; and to recompense injury with kindness.”
philosophy.explanation: Laozi lists returning kindness for injury as part of the way of the Tao.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's demand to do good to those who have done harm.
philosophy.source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching 63 (trans. James Legge)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close match on recompensing injury with kindness.

kurals.tamil:
இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும்
திண்மைஉண் டாகப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inmai oruvarku ilivandru saalbennum
thinmaiun daakap perin.
kurals.meaning: Poverty is no disgrace to a person who possesses the inner strength called perfection of character.
kurals.elementary: Some people have lots of toys and money, and some have very little. Valluvar says having little is nothing to be ashamed of, as long as you are honest, kind and strong inside. That inner strength is worth more than any treasure.
kurals.university: Inmai (இன்மை, 'having nothing, poverty') is not ilivu (இளிவு, 'disgrace') for one who has gained the thinmai (திண்மை, 'firmness, solidity') called saalbu. The image of perfection as a kind of solidity anticipates the stability of Kural 989. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all read inmai as material poverty, and Karunanidhi adds that such a person treats saalbu itself as wealth; Sivayogi Sivakumar widens inmai to 'hardships'. Textual note: ytamizh.com reads இளிவன்று (ilivandru, 'is not disgrace'), the standard reading supported by the commentaries' gloss இழிவு; thirukkural.net's main text prints இனிவன்று, which appears to be a typographical error (ன for ள), since its own commentaries gloss the word as இழிவு. This edition follows இளிவன்று. Placed just before the chapters on Nalkuravu (Poverty, ch. 105) and Iravu (Begging, ch. 106), the couplet establishes that character, not wealth, sets the limits of dignity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, a poor brahmin friend of Krishna's boyhood (known in later tradition as Sudama or Kuchela), content and self-controlled despite his poverty, visits Krishna at Dvaraka carrying only a handful of flattened rice; Krishna receives him with great honour.
hinduism.explanation: The story shows that the poor man's devotion and contentment made him worthy of the highest honour despite his lack of wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents poverty as no disgrace to a person of firm character.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; the name Sudama comes from later tradition rather than the Bhagavata text itself, and the story stresses devotion more than character.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb ranks an upright poor person above a rich person of crooked ways.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: integrity removes any shame from poverty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a near one-to-one match.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that real wealth lies in inner contentment, not in property.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it relocates worth from possessions to inner strength.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a strong match on inner wealth, though it speaks of contentment rather than moral perfection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot, as it is said: “You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors, you shall be happy and you shall prosper” (Psalms 128:2)”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as being content with what one has.
judaism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's view that lack of possessions does not diminish a person of firm character.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (quoted from the middle of the mishnah); good match on redefining wealth, though it speaks of contentment rather than character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names contentment as the greatest wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it implies that a person rich in inner qualities is not truly poor.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a reasonable match on inner wealth, without the Kural's explicit point about poverty and disgrace.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami, having renounced his kingdom, tells the disguised god Indra that he lives happily owning nothing, so even the burning of his former city costs him nothing.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that having nothing is no disgrace, and even a joy, to one of firm spiritual character.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on dignity in having nothing, though Nami's poverty is chosen renunciation (aparigraha) rather than misfortune.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “... I have no time to give either to any public matter of interest or to any concern of my own, but I am in utter poverty by reason of my devotion to the god.”

kurals.tamil:
ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம்பெயரார் சான்றாண்மைக்கு
ஆழி எனப்படு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oozhi peyarinum thaampeyaraar saandraanmaikku
aazhi enappadu vaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who are called the ocean of perfect character will not change, even if the ages themselves change.
kurals.elementary: A big rock on the beach stays in the same place year after year while the waves, the weather and the people all change around it. Valluvar says truly good people are like that: whatever happens around them, they stay good.
kurals.university: Oozhi (ஊழி) is the cosmic age or aeon, and its 'shifting' (peyarinum, பெயரினும், 'even if it moves') evokes the dissolution at the end of an age, when, in Indian cosmology, the seas break their bounds. Against this, those called aazhi (ஆழி) of saandraanmai do not shift (thaam peyaraar, தாம்பெயரார்). Aazhi can mean either 'ocean' or 'shore, boundary', and the commentators divide: Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi take it as ocean ('the ocean of perfection'), while Pappaiah and Kesikan, with Pope ('of perfect virtue's sea the shore'), read it as the shore that holds the sea in, an image which sharpens the contrast, since the shore holds even when the seas of the age-end overflow. Pope's line 'Who, though the fates should fail' renders oozhi loosely as fate. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads oozhi as ordinary change over time. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who is not disturbed by the incessant flow of desires – that enter like rivers into the ocean, which is ever being filled but is always still – can alone achieve peace, and not the man who strives to satisfy such desires.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares the steady sage to the ocean, which stays unmoved though rivers pour into it constantly.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same ocean image for the noble person who stays unchanged through every change.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.70 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a strong match on the image of the unmoved ocean, applied in the Gita to desire rather than to the turning of ages.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm describes the righteous person who keeps his word even at a cost and promises that he will never be moved.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it portrays the person of integrity as one who 'changeth not' and stands firm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; strong match on unchanging integrity, though without the cosmic scale of the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah" and then remained on a right course - the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised.”

judaism.quote_or_event: “A song of ascents. Those who trust in GOD are like Mount Zion that cannot be moved, enduring forever.”

judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Revised JPS 2023); good match on immovability, grounded in trust in God rather than in character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the wise person to a rock that the storm cannot shake.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the perfected person as unmoved by whatever changes around them.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a strong match on unshakability, applied to praise and blame rather than to the turning of ages.

jainism.quote_or_event: “... difficult to attack like a lion, steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean, mild like the moon, refulgent like the sun, pure like excellent gold; like the earth he patiently bore everything; like a well-kindled fire he shone in his splendour.”
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes the houseless Mahavira through a series of similes, including the steadiness of Mount Mandara and the depth of the ocean.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's 'ocean of perfection', it pictures the perfected one as deep as the ocean and immovable as the world-mountain.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (excerpted with ellipsis); a strong match, sharing the ocean image and steadiness, though it describes one Jina rather than the noble in general.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odyssey XX, Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own house and enraged by the suitors' insolence, strikes his breast and tells his heart to endure, reminding it that it endured worse in the Cyclops' cave; he holds firm until the right moment.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus stays steady in purpose through twenty years of upheaval.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His steadfastness under changing fortunes echoes the Kural's noble person who does not change when the age changes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; next-best match, since Odysseus' endurance is strategic self-control rather than unchanging moral perfection.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius urges himself to stand firm like a headland that the waves cannot move.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's image, especially in the reading of aazhi as the shore that holds while the seas surge.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong match in both image and meaning.

kurals.tamil:
சான்றவர் சான்றாண்மை குன்றின் இருநிலந்தான்
தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Saandravar saandraanmai kundrin irunilandhaan
thaangaadhu manno porai.
kurals.meaning: If the noble were to fall short in their nobility, even this great earth could not bear its burden.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a big table held up by a few strong legs. If those legs get weak, everything on the table comes crashing down. Valluvar says good people are like those legs for the whole world: if they stop being good, the world cannot hold itself up.
kurals.university: The closing couplet extends saandraanmai from personal virtue to cosmic support. If the saandravar (சான்றவர், 'the perfected') should decline (kundrin, குன்றின்) in their saandraanmai, the 'great earth' (irunilam, இருநிலம்) itself could not bear (thaangaadhu, தாங்காது) its porai (பொறை, 'burden'); manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan read porai as the earth's burden, so that the noble become, with the five pillars of Kural 983, the hidden supports of the world; Karunanidhi instead takes porai as 'patience', reading that the world would not patiently tolerate such a decline. Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of irunilam as the 'two states' of inner and outer life is idiosyncratic. Pope: 'The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease, / If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease.' The idea that the righteous sustain the world appears in many traditions, and here completes the chapter's arc from personal duty (981) to the stability of the world. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If I did not perform prescribed duties, all these worlds would be put to ruination. I would be the cause of creating unwanted population, and I would thereby destroy the peace of all living beings.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that if he, the exemplar, ceased doing his duty, the worlds would fall into ruin, since others follow the example of the great.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the stability of the world to the continued right conduct of its noblest figures.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.24 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a strong structural match, though the Gita speaks of the divine exemplar while the Kural speaks of noble human beings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls his disciples the salt that preserves the earth and warns of what happens if they lose their quality.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the good the preservers of the world and warns of the consequences if their goodness fails.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a close match on the righteous as the world's preservative and the danger of their decline.

islam.quote_or_event: “And your Lord would not have destroyed the cities unjustly while their people were reformers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that God does not destroy communities while they contain people who work for good.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it suggests that the presence of the righteous keeps the world from ruin.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the alquran.cloud API; good match on the righteous as protection against ruin, framed as divine judgment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he said, “Let not my Sovereign be angry if I speak but this last time: What if ten should be found there?” “I will not destroy, for the sake of the ten,” came the reply.”
judaism.explanation: Abraham bargains with God over Sodom, and God agrees to spare the city for the sake of just ten righteous people.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the fate of a whole community resting on a few righteous people.

judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Revised JPS 2023); a strong match on the righteous few sustaining the many, at the level of a city rather than the whole earth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern. If these two bright qualities did not guard the world, there would be no recognition of 'mother' here, no recognition of 'mother's sister,' 'uncle's wife,' 'teacher's wife,' or 'wife of those who deserve respect.' ...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that conscience and concern (hiri and ottappa) are the guardians of the world, without which social order would collapse.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the moral qualities of people are what hold the world together.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.9, Lokapala Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (abridged with ellipsis); a strong match on virtue sustaining the world, centred on two qualities rather than on noble persons.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The most excellent twice-born men who possess these good qualities, are able to save themselves and others.”
jainism.explanation: At the end of his account of the true Brahmana, the monk Jayaghosha says that only those with real virtues can save both themselves and others.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the welfare of others depend on the virtue of the perfected few.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best match only, since it speaks of saving others spiritually rather than of the earth bearing its burden, and Jain cosmology does not make the world's physical stability depend on the virtuous.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Works and Days, Hesiod contrasts the city of the just, where peace, plenty and healthy children flourish under Zeus' favour, with the city of the unjust, on which Zeus sends famine, plague and ruin, so that even one wicked man can bring suffering on a whole city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that the prosperity or ruin of a community follows the justice of its people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the well-being of the world to the virtue of those in it.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-247 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; good match on communal fate following justice, applied to a city rather than the whole earth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that until philosophers rule, or rulers become genuine lovers of wisdom, cities and the human race will have no rest from their evils.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that the well-being of human society depends on the wise and good being at its centre.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the fate of the world hinge on the presence of perfected people.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim in this session; a reasonable match on the good as the world's support, framed politically rather than morally.
